newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FDA warns that AIDS drug may cause diabetes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FDA warns that AIDS drug may cause diabetes.

text.p: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration warned doctors on Wednesday that the new class of AIDS drug known as protease inhibitors may contribute to diabetes.
But the FDA said that problems related to diabetes occur relatively infrequently, and said it did not recommend that patients forego protease inhibitor therapy.

"FDA today warned physicians that protease inhibitors may contribute to increases in blood sugar and even diabetes in HIV patients and recommended close monitoring of their glucose levels," the agency said in a statement.

The FDA said it sent a letter to doctors noting that it had received 83 reported cases of new or exacerbated diabetes and hyperglycemia -- increased blood sugar levels -- in HIV-infected patients taking one of the drugs.
Protease inhibitors work by blocking HIV -- the virus that causes AIDS -- from leaving a patient's DNA and invading the rest of the body.
Used as part of a three-drug combination, the drugs have dramatically improved the health of many AIDS patients, in some cases driving down the viral load to nondetectable levels.

About 150,000 Americans take one of the four approved protease drugs -- Merck & Co's Crixivan (indinavir), Hoffmann-La Roche's Invirase (saquinavir), Abbott Laboratories' Norvir (ritonavir) and Agouron Pharmaceuticals' Viracept (nelfinavir).

FDA medical officer Jeff Murray characterized the incidence of hyperglycemia -- which has been seen equally across all the drugs -- as "infrequent," occurring in less than one percent of patients taking the drugs. If caught early, Murray said, the high blood sugar can be managed through insulin or oral hypoglycemic medications. This is the primary reason for notifying physicians.
"We're saying it's up to a doctor's clinical judgement," said Murray, adding that doctors will have to strike a balance between treating HIV and symptoms of high blood sugar.
Of the 83 reported cases, 27 required hospitalization. There were six life-threatening incidents, including five ketoacidosis attacks, which can result in coma or death.

Blood sugar began to rise as soon as four days after therapy began, with an average onset time of 76 days. Murray said the hyperglycemic effects are eventually reversible, but that some patients continue to take oral anti-diabetes drugs.

The reversibility suggests there may be a link between protease drugs and elevated blood sugar, but there is no definite link, emphasized Murray. There was no indication in trials that hyperglycemia might be a side effect, but that is not surprising given that it is an infrequent event, he said.

Protease manufacturers are being required to warn about diabetes. Merck spokesman Michael Seggev said his firm plans to quickly add the warning to its prescribing information and to all information for physicians and patients.

Agouron said there have been two reports of hyperglycemia among the 30,000 Americans taking Viracept, approved March 14. An Agouron spokeswoman said the firm is "amending our package insert and promotional material to incorporate this warning."
